client: Lately, I've been waking up in the middle of the night with this tight feeling in my chest, thinking about all the exams coming up. Hearing my classmates talk about their 12-hour study sessions makes me feel like I'm already falling behind, even though classes just started. I don't know if talking about it will help - it's not like therapy can change how much work I have to do.
therapist: I hear the worry and pressure in your voice as you talk about these nighttime anxieties and comparisons with classmates. While therapy can't reduce your workload, we can work on how you're interpreting these challenges - the thoughts that "I'm already falling behind" might be adding extra stress on top of the actual demands. How does that resonate with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about my thoughts adding extra stress, but it's hard not to feel behind when I see my classmates handling everything so well. The anxiety feels real because the workload is actually overwhelming - it's not just in my head.
therapist: I can hear the heaviness in your voice as you describe this - it sounds like you're caught between acknowledging your feelings while also dismissing them as "not real" because the workload is objectively large. Let me ask: when you see classmates appearing to handle things well, what makes you certain they're not feeling just as overwhelmed but hiding it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: You're right, I do feel this tension between acknowledging my feelings and dismissing them. When I see classmates handling things well, I guess I assume they must be fine because they’re not collapsing under the pressure like I am. It’s hard to imagine they could be struggling just as much but hiding it—it feels like I’m the only one who can’t keep up.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained as you describe this - it seems like comparing yourself to others is leaving you feeling isolated in your struggle. That belief that "I'm the only one who can't keep up" must feel very heavy to carry alone - what evidence do you have that others aren't just putting on a brave face too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I never really thought about other people just pretending to have it together. But when I see my coworkers laughing at lunch or friends posting perfect vacation photos, it's hard to imagine they're struggling like me. I still feel like I'm the only one who's barely keeping my head above water. 

Even if they are faking it, that doesn't really make me feel better - it just makes me feel like I'm worse at hiding my problems than everyone else.
therapist: Your voice sounds rushed and quiet as you share this - it seems like admitting these feelings brings up a sense of vulnerability and self-criticism. It might help to gently challenge the idea that struggling openly means you're "worse" at handling things - could it instead show courage in acknowledging your humanity?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I never thought of it that way before. It does feel vulnerable to admit I’m struggling, and I worry people will see me as weak or incompetent. But the idea that it could be courageous instead… that’s kind of hard for me to believe right now. It feels more like I’m just failing at keeping it together.
therapist: Your voice sounds shaky and hesitant as you share this - I can hear how much effort it takes to even consider this new perspective. It's okay if believing in your own courage feels out of reach right now - what matters is that you're willing to explore these feelings at all, even when it feels uncomfortable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: It’s hard to believe I’m courageous when I feel so stuck and scared most of the time. I want to explore these feelings, but it’s frustrating because it feels like I’m not making progress—like I’m just spinning in circles. I guess part of me doubts that talking about it will actually change anything.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and rushed as you describe this - I can hear both the fear and frustration in feeling stuck. That doubt about whether talking helps is understandable, yet here you are, still showing up and working through these difficult feelings - that persistence itself might be more meaningful than you realize right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess it does feel good that I'm still trying, even when it's hard. But sometimes I wonder if I'm just going in circles—like I'll never really get past this anxiety. It's exhausting to feel this way all the time, and I don't know if talking about it actually changes anything. 

The worst part is when people say "just relax" or "think positive" like it's that simple. It makes me feel even more broken because I can't seem to do that no matter how hard I try.
therapist: Your voice sounds urgent and strained as you share this—I can hear how deeply frustrating and exhausting this cycle feels for you. Those well-meaning but simplistic suggestions must feel especially painful when you're already trying so hard—let's explore what "getting past this" would realistically look like for you, rather than just "thinking positive."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, it’s just... I don’t even know what "getting past this" would look like anymore. People keep telling me to just push through or distract myself, but the anxiety always comes back worse. It’s like I’m stuck in this loop where even trying to imagine a way out makes me feel exhausted before I even start.
therapist: Your voice sounds higher and more strained as you describe this—I can hear how trapped and worn down you feel by this cycle. When even imagining a way forward feels exhausting, it makes sense that you'd question whether change is possible—but let's explore together what small, manageable steps might look like, rather than pushing through or distracting. How does that sound?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly the idea of even small steps feels overwhelming right now. When I try to imagine doing something different, my brain just floods with "what ifs" about failing or looking stupid. It's like my body physically tenses up at the thought.
therapist: Your voice sounds tight and rushed as you describe this—I can hear how those "what ifs" create both mental and physical tension for you. Let's gently explore this together: when those thoughts about failing or looking stupid come up, what evidence do you have that those fears would definitely come true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know, it just feels like the evidence doesn't matter because the fear is so overwhelming in the moment. Like last week when I had to give that presentation at work—I knew statistically I'd probably be fine, but my hands shook so badly I could barely hold my notes. It's not rational but it feels so real when it's happening.
therapist: Your voice sounds rushed and quiet as you describe this experience—I can hear how powerless those overwhelming moments make you feel, even when you know logically the fears might be exaggerated. That gap between knowing something statistically and feeling it emotionally is so frustrating—let's explore how we might help bridge that divide in a way that feels manageable for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
